title: RNA 5-Methylcytosine (m5C) in Cancer: An Emerging Epitranscriptomic Hub for Therapy Resistance and Clinical Translation.
abstract: RNA 5-methylcytosine (m5C) has emerged as an important epitranscriptomic modification in cancer. Rather than acting as a uniformly oncogenic mark, m5C produces context-dependent effects by coupling RNA fate to cellular adaptation. Through control of RNA stability, nuclear export, translation, splicing, and RNA structure, the m5C machinery connects therapeutic stress to DNA damage repair, redox homeostasis, metabolic plasticity, cancer stemness, and tumor-immune interactions. Here, we synthesize the molecular basis of and detection of RNA m5C, distinguish causal from associative evidence, and examine how m5C-dependent RNA regulation contributes to tumor progression and resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy responses. We also discuss tumor-suppressive and context-dependent activities of individual NSUN proteins, cross-talk with other epigenetic and epitranscriptomic pathways, and the methodological limitations that complicate m5C mapping. Current m5C-directed compounds remain preclinical; therefore, their most immediate value lies in mechanistic validation and biomarker development rather than established clinical use. A rigorous, method-aware framework will be essential for determining when m5C is a driver, a permissive adaptation, or a correlate of therapeutic resistance.

title: Protocol for whole-mount staining of melanized insect tissues for RNA and protein detection.
abstract: Technical barriers have limited whole-mount staining and imaging of internal tissues in many insects and other arthropods. Here, we present a protocol for whole-mount staining of melanized insect tissues for RNA and protein detection. We describe steps for preparing, permeabilizing, and bleaching samples; designing RNA probes; and staining. We then detail procedures for imaging samples. This protocol is compatible with both immunohistochemistry and fluorescence in situ hybridization and enables high-resolution microscopy of tissues surrounded by cuticle without sectioning. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Glotzer et al.1.

title: Plant molecular farming: from gene design to scalable expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins.
abstract: Plant-based expression systems have emerged as low-cost, scalable, and safe alternatives for producing therapeutic recombinant proteins. Among them, Nicotiana benthamiana stands out as a versatile chassis due to its rapid growth, high biomass, efficient transient expression, and weak RNA silencing. In this review, we systematically summarize the key technical procedures and recent advances in the expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins in N. benthamiana, covering gene design and subcellular targeting, expression vector engineering and delivery, host engineering for enhanced yield, and cultivation optimization. We discuss strategies to address major bottlenecks, including codon optimization, endoplasmic reticulum retention, protease knockout, glycoengineering to eliminate immunogenic plant-specific glycans, and the use of viral-based transient expression systems such as magnICON, pEAQ-HT, and geminiviral replicons. Additionally, we highlight emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based multiplexed chassis engineering, artificial intelligence-assisted vector design, and hydroponic cultivation for scalable production. Despite significant progress, challenges remain in achieving coordinated high-level expression of multiple proteins and reducing downstream processing costs. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the current state and future directions of plant molecular farming in N. benthamiana, emphasizing its irreplaceable value for rapid emergency response, personalized vaccines, and safe biopharmaceutical manufacturing.

title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
abstract: Spatial epigenomics maps chromatin states within intact tissues, yet current methods remain limited by accessibility and scale. We developed SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag framework that converts epigenetic marks-associated DNA into polyadenylated RNA through T7 based linear amplification, enabling direct integration with standard spatial transcriptomic workflows. Applied to the mouse brain, SPACETag resolved activating and repressive chromatin landscapes, recovered region-specific gene regulatory programs across anatomical domains, and showed strong correlation with existing bulk and single cell reference data. We generated an integrated multimodal atlas of the aging mouse brain, profiling five histone modifications and the transcriptome in parallel across the adult lifespan to establish the largest spatial multimodal dataset to date. This analysis uncovered sharp regional divergence with aging in the brain: fiber tracts showed widespread transcriptional downregulation, often without nearby chromatin state transitions, whereas the isocortex showed coordinated chromatin transcriptome changes, including an H3K4me1 peak module that increased with age, was enriched at super-enhancers and linked to upregulation of neuronal plasticity regulators. These findings highlight the power of multimodal and high throughput spatial genomics in uncovering the divergent regulatory logic that governs tissue-specific vulnerability and resilience in the aging brain.

title: The deubiquitinase PSMD14 accelerates cervical cancer progression, with thiolutin offering a novel therapeutic approach.
abstract: Abnormal function of deubiquitination enzymes is implicated in cancer progression. However, the role of the 26S proteasome non-ATPase regulatory subunit 14 (PSMD14) in cervical cancer development and its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In our study, we evaluated the role of PSMD14 in the progression of cervical cancer. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were used to measure differentially expressed PSMD14 in cervical cancer tissues and normal cervical tissues. PSMD14 knockdown and overexpression were performed to investigate the functional role of PSMD14 in vitro and in vivo. The expression and regulation of PSMD14 and PTBP1 were evaluated using immunoprecipitation, western blot analysis. Flow cytometry apoptosis assay was used to detect the cytotoxic effect of THL on cervical cancer cells. PSMD14 is significantly overexpressed in cervical cancer tissues compared to normal cervical tissues. Overexpression of PSMD14 was correlated with myometrial invasion depth and histological classification in cervical cancer patients. Knockdown of PSMD14 in cervical cancer cells led to a significant reduction in proliferation and invasion capabilities in vitro, whereas its overexpression promoted these malignant phenotypes. In a xenograft mouse model, PSMD14 knockdown inhibited tumor growth. Mechanistically, we identified that PSMD14 directly interacts with PTBP1, an RNA-binding protein highly expressed in cervical cancer tissues. Knockdown PSMD14 resulted in decreased PTBP1 protein expression. Notably, we explored the therapeutic potential of THL, a specific inhibitor of PSMD14. THL treatment effectively suppressed cervical cancer cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro, and significantly inhibited tumor growth in vivo without observable toxicity. In summary, our findings reveal an oncogenic role of PSMD14 in cervical cancer progression, highlighting its potential as a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target.

title: FMRP safeguards long mRNA expression by opposing repressive RNP states
abstract: Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) is widely viewed as a translational repressor, yet its loss paradoxically compromises expression of exceptionally long, dosage-sensitive neurodevelopmental mRNAs. First shown in Drosophila oocytes, this selective loss extends to mouse cortex and hippocampus, but its mechanism remains unknown. Here, we uncover a protective function for FMRP: shielding long mRNAs from repression by Me31B/DDX6, a conserved RNA helicase that organizes repressive RNP complexes. In Drosophila oocytes, FMRP loss redirects target mRNAs into Me31B-marked P-bodies. Transcriptome-wide binding maps reveal extensive FMRP-Me31B co-occupancy, preferentially concentrated on long coding sequences whose translation depends on FMRP. Strikingly, disrupting Me31B-dependent repression preferentially enhances translation of FMRP targets in FMRP-deficient oocytes. We identify Rin/G3BP, Caprin, and Lig/UBAP2L as FMRP-associated cofactors supporting expression of distinct targets. Together, our findings challenge the prevailing view of FMRP as a translational repressor, revealing instead a mechanism that safeguards vulnerable neurodevelopmental mRNAs from inappropriate cytoplasmic silencing.

title: Targeting MDA5 induces immunogenic cell death and promotes anti-tumor immunity.
abstract: Identifying targets to enhance tumor immunity is an urgent need. Although nucleic acid sensors play critical roles in promoting tumor immune clearance, their exceptionally low mutation rate in cancers suggests potential unexplored roles in tumor progression. Here, we demonstrate that the RNA sensor melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5) promotes immune evasion, and its high expression is strongly predictive of poor survival and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy in patients. Targeting MDA5 reshapes the tumor microenvironment, strengthening immune memory responses and enhancing effector CD8⁺ T cell activity in preclinical models in female mice. Mechanistically, MDA5 deficiency triggers unfolded protein response driven immunogenic cell death through induction of damage-associated molecular patterns, leading to enhanced dendritic cell-mediated antigen engulfment and T cell activation. Additionally, MDA5 loss primes the ASK1-JNK/P38 signaling pathway, sensitizing tumor cells to TNF-α/IFN-γ, further amplifying this process. Consequently, targeting MDA5 enhances the efficacy of ICB therapy across multiple cancer types, positioning it as a promising therapeutic target.

title: Unraveling the complexities of cardiorenal syndrome: epigenetic and post-translational modification perspectives.
abstract: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is a complex condition where heart and kidney dysfunctions interact, leading to high morbidity and mortality. It presents significant challenges in cardiovascular and renal medicine due to its prevalence and severe outcomes. Traditional models focus on hemodynamic issues, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation, oxidative stress, and inflammation but fall short in explaining CRS's chronic and varied nature. Recent research in epigenomics and proteomics highlights the importance of epigenetic regulation and post-translational modifications (PTMs) in CRS development. Epigenetics provides stable, long-term gene regulation related to diseases without changing the DNA sequence, mainly through DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA regulation. In contrast, PTMs quickly alter protein function and signaling via ubiquitination, phosphorylation, acetylation, and newer processes like lactoylation and carbamylation. Both play key roles in CRS by affecting inflammation, fibrosis, and mitochondrial dysfunction, and are linked through a complex regulatory network. This review details the mechanisms and interactions between epigenetics and PTMs in CRS, emphasizing their potential as biomarkers and therapeutic targets, and discusses research limitations and future directions to advance understanding.

title: 2-methylbutanal remodels arachidonic acid metabolism and antitumor immunity through ENO1 in colorectal cancer.
abstract: Active aldehydes are increasingly recognized as bioactive metabolites, but their roles in tumor immune regulation remain poorly defined. In colorectal cancer (CRC), prostaglandin metabolism contributes to immune suppression, whereas its upstream metabolic regulators are incompletely understood. Here, we investigated 2-methylbutanal (2-MBTL), a branched-chain small-molecule aldehyde, in CRC. The antitumor and immunoregulatory effects of 2-methylbutanal (2-MBTL) were examined in CRC cell systems and mouse models. Its molecular target and downstream pathway were investigated using target-identification assays, RNA interaction analyses, genetic manipulation, transcriptomic profiling, and PGE2 supplementation. 2-MBTL suppressed CRC growth at well-tolerated doses, increased tumor immunogenic signals, enhanced intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and effector activity, and reduced suppressive myeloid populations. Its direct antiproliferative effect was limited, whereas its antitumor activity was markedly weakened in immunodeficient mice or after CD8⁺ T-cell depletion. Mechanistically, 2-MBTL bound ENO1 and impaired its association with YAP1 mRNA, reducing YAP1 protein expression without substantially altering ENO1 abundance or glycolysis-associated readouts. This was accompanied by increased HPGD expression and reduced PGE2 levels. ENO1 overexpression attenuated the effects of 2-MBTL, while exogenous PGE2 partially reversed tumor suppression and immune remodeling. In human CRC tissues, ENO1 and HPGD showed opposing associations with CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and survival. 2-MBTL also enhanced the efficacy of PD-1 blockade. 2-MBTL promotes CD8⁺ T-cell-dependent antitumor immunity by modulating ENO1-associated post-transcriptional regulation and suppressing YAP1-related PGE2 metabolism.

title: Integrative Network Pharmacology and Transcriptomic Analysis Prioritizes CCR1 and C5AR1 as Candidate Thromboinflammatory Targets Shared by Panax notoginseng Saponins and Stroke-Relevant Drugs in Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Thromboinflammation is a central pathological process contributing to secondary brain injury after ischemic stroke (IS). Panax notoginseng saponins (PNS) exert pleiotropic anti-inflammatory, antithrombotic, and vascular effects, but the molecular convergence between PNS-associated pharmacology and stroke-relevant conventional agents remains incompletely characterized. We integrated network pharmacology, bulk transcriptomic datasets, single-cell RNA sequencing, regulatory-network analysis, and structure-based molecular docking to prioritize candidate targets shared by PNS and an exploratory screening panel of 16 stroke-relevant pharmacological agents. Predicted drug and PNS targets were intersected with IS-associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs), followed by network analysis, independent cross-dataset expression assessment, gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA), transcription-factor (TF) prediction with co-expression analysis, myeloid-cell sub-clustering, and GNINA docking. The screening framework yielded 79 shared predicted pharmacological targets and 10 disease-associated candidates: ITK, CDK2, C5AR1, VDR, S1PR2, KIF11, CCR1, FAP, PRKCD, and MAOA. CCR1 and C5AR1 were prioritized because they combined high network connectivity with consistent disease-associated expression across the analyzed datasets and strong links to thromboinflammatory pathways. BATF2 and SPI1 expression positively correlated with both C5AR1 and CCR1 in GSE56267. Myeloid sub-clustering further showed that C5ar1 was broadly distributed across stroke-associated microglial and monocyte/macrophage states, whereas Ccr1 was more restricted to activated inflammatory and infiltrating myeloid populations. GNINA docking of all fourteen network-defined receptor-ligand systems identified five complexes with docking affinity scores between - 8.06 and - 10.94 kcal/mol (ginsenosides Rd and Re at CCR1; notoginsenoside R1, ginsenoside Rg1, and ginsenoside Rd at C5AR1). Collectively, these analyses prioritize CCR1 and C5AR1 as convergent candidate thromboinflammatory nodes shared by PNS-associated and stroke-relevant pharmacological target spaces. The findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish pharmacological synergy, direct receptor coupling, or causal therapeutic mechanisms.

title: Divergent roles of H3K18 lactylation in human diseases: metabolic-epigenetic circuits and translational challenges.
abstract: Histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la) links fluctuations in lactate metabolism with chromatin-dependent transcription. Promoter- and enhancer-level associations suggest that H3K18la can report local metabolic-chromatin coupling, but evidence for modification-specific causality remains uneven because the known writers and erasers are promiscuous, dedicated readers are poorly defined, and broad acyltransferase inhibitors perturb competing histone and non-histone marks. Across tumor, inflammatory, metabolic, cardiovascular, and degenerative-disease models, H3K18la participates in oncogenic, immunoregulatory, fibrotic, or reparative programs according to cell lineage, chromatin state, metabolic exposure, and disease stage. We synthesize these observations using a testable framework in which lactate and lactyl-CoA provide metabolic permission, whereas transcription factors, chromatin accessibility, histone chaperones, and candidate protein or RNA scaffolds provide locus selection; downstream readers or conventional transcriptional effectors then shape the biological output. Direct long non-coding RNA (lncRNA)-guided deposition and a universally validated H3K18la reader remain unproven. Human cohort data support exploratory, disease-specific associations, but assay heterogeneity and the lack of prospective external validation preclude current clinical use. Progress will require histone H3 lysine 18 acetylation (H3K18ac)-aware, inhibitor-independent causal tests, structural validation of readers, integrated chromatin-RNA profiling, and prospective multicenter cohorts.

title: An ICAM1⁺ inflammatory fibroblast state in atrial fibrillation and metabolic-stress-associated atrial remodeling.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is associated with inflammatory and fibrotic atrial remodeling, but the fibroblast states connecting these processes remain incompletely defined. ICAM1 is a key inflammatory adhesion molecule, yet its cell-state context within atrial fibroblast heterogeneity remains unclear. Reanalysis of human left atrial single-cell RNA sequencing data identified an ICAM1⁺ inflammatory fibroblast state that was not detected among fibroblasts from sinus rhythm samples in this dataset and represented 17.3% of fibroblasts in AF samples. Trajectory inference, pathway enrichment, and co-expression network analysis associated this state with inflammatory and matrix-remodeling programs. In diet-induced obesity (DIO) mice, susceptibility to burst pacing-induced AF-like atrial tachyarrhythmia episodes was higher than in normal-diet controls (5/8 vs. 0/8 mice; Fisher's exact P = 0.0256), accompanied by left atrial remodeling. RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization supported increased Icam1 expression in Tcf21⁺ fibroblast-associated stromal cells. ICAM1 protein was increased in CD140a-enriched atrial fibroblast fractions from DIO mice (relative ICAM1/β-actin: 2.70 ± 0.46 vs. 1.00 ± 0.15; P = 0.0001). In primary human cardiac fibroblasts, ICAM1 knockdown reduced migration under TGF-β1-stimulated conditions (49.90 ± 1.63% vs. 20.44 ± 1.51% wound closure; P < 0.0001), and reduced α-SMA and Collagen I fluorescence signals. Lentiviral TNXB overexpression partially restored Fibronectin and Collagen I expression under ICAM1-knockdown conditions (Fibronectin: 2.26 ± 0.21-fold vs. 4.11 ± 0.28-fold, P < 0.0001; Collagen I: 1.09 ± 0.06-fold vs. 1.54 ± 0.09-fold, P = 0.0004). This study identifies an AF-enriched ICAM1⁺ inflammatory fibroblast state associated with inflammatory-matrix remodeling programs. The findings support Icam1 upregulation in fibroblast-associated atrial stromal cells during DIO-associated remodeling and link ICAM1 perturbation to altered fibroblast migration and selected TNXB-associated matrix-protein readouts. Further fibroblast-specific and clinically annotated studies are needed to define causality and translational relevance.

title: Alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN) of Vibrio fischeri is required during initial squid light organ colonization but its continued induction is not required for maintenance.
abstract: Animals depend on bacterial symbionts that provide functions essential for host physiology and fitness. The marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri establishes a mutualistic association within the light organ of the Hawaiian bobtail squid Euprymna scolopes, where bacterial bioluminescence enables a host camouflage behavior. Successful colonization of the light organ requires the alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN), which activates genes involved in biofilm formation and motility that are essential for bacterial entry into the host. However, whether σ54 remains important after the initial stages of colonization has been unclear. Here, using an IPTG-inducible rpoN expression system, we demonstrate that induction of rpoN is required for initial entry into the light organ, but continued inducer exposure is not required for subsequent maintenance of colonization and bioluminescence production. Transcriptomic analysis of RNA-sequencing of low-cell-density cultures identified σ54-dependent expression of genes involved in flagellar motility, chemotaxis, nitrogen assimilation, molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis, and formate metabolism. We further show that the bacterial enhancer-binding protein VF_1401 activates genes required for Moco biosynthesis and formate metabolism but is not required for light organ colonization. Together, these findings define the temporal requirement for σ54 during symbiosis establishment and reveal a previously unrecognized role for σ54 in regulating molybdenum-dependent metabolism in V. fischeri.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria encode the alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN), which enables selective activation of specific cellular processes in response to environmental signals. Our findings refine the conditions under which σ54 contributes to host colonization by a bacterial symbiont, providing new insight into the context-dependent roles of this conserved regulator. In addition, our transcriptomic analysis identifies a previously unrecognized link between σ54 and molybdenum assimilation, revealing a potential mechanism by which σ54 coordinates trace element homeostasis with bacterial physiology. These findings broaden our understanding of σ54 regulatory networks and may inform future strategies to manipulate the physiology of beneficial bacterial symbionts.

title: WTAP regulates PTEN through m6A methylation to modulate the inflammatory response in CD4+ T cells from patients with ankylosing spondylitis.
abstract: This study aimed to investigate how Wilms' tumour 1-related protein (WTAP)-mediated m6A methylation regulates PTEN and thereby influences the inflammatory response in ankylosing spondylitis (AS) through a combination of a case-control study and cellular experiments. The study enrolled 45 AS patients and 45 age- and gender-matched healthy controls. Peripheral venous blood (10 mL) was drawn from each participant, and CD4+ T lymphocytes were isolated using a human positive selection kit. mRNA expression levels of WTAP and PTEN were measured by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Plasma was separated by centrifugation and subjected to enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to quantify inflammatory cytokine concentrations. A WTAP-knockdown model was established in human Jurkat T cells using small interfering RNA (siRNA), followed by analysis of downstream gene transcription and protein expression via qRT-PCR and Western blotting, respectively. After WTAP knockdown, the m6A modification level of PTEN mRNA in Jurkat cells was determined by MeRIP-qPCR. Results showed that WTAP and PTEN expression levels in CD4+ T lymphocytes were significantly downregulated in AS patients compared to healthy controls, and both were inversely correlated with TNF-α levels. Moreover, WTAP knockdown in Jurkat T cells led to a marked decrease in both PTEN expression and its m6A modification, which coincided with a significant increase in TNF-α expression. In conclusion, WTAP downregulation promotes AS inflammation by decreasing PTEN expression through an m6A-dependent mechanism.

title: SHP1-Mediated FTO Dephosphorylation Regulates Mitophagy and Promotes Tumor Progression via N(6)-Methyladenosine in Colorectal Cancer.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) progression and resistance to therapy are driven by complex molecular mechanisms, implying the importance of identifying biomarkers and developing treatment strategies. Whereas Src homology region 2 domain-containing phosphatase 1 (SHP1) is implicated in immune regulation, its role in tumor malignancy remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that SHP1 is significantly upregulated in CRC tissues and correlates with poor prognosis. Mechanistically, SHP1 was found to dephosphorylate the N(6)-methyladenosine (m6A) demethylase fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) at the Y475 tyrosine residue, thereby enhancing its enzymatic activity to reduce global m6A methylation levels. Integrated RNA sequencing and m6A profiling revealed that SHP1 depletion increased PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) mRNA m6A modifications, promoting its degradation and suppressing mitophagy. SHP1 inhibitor TPI-1 or siRNA-SHP1-loaded lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) attenuated CRC cell proliferation, migration, and tumor growth in xenograft models through impaired mitochondrial homeostasis. These findings establish the SHP1-FTO-m6A axis as a critical regulator of mitophagy-driven CRC progression. Clinically, our study highlights SHP1 as a prognostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target, with TPI-1 and LNP-siSHP1 offering novel strategies for CRC management.

title: Esco2 restrains pathological endothelial-mesenchymal transition through hidden isoform regulation in a Roberts syndrome model.
abstract: Roberts syndrome is caused by biallelic ESCO2 pathogenic variants, but the mechanisms linking ESCO2 loss to embryonic endothelial failure remain poorly defined. Endothelial cells must maintain identity and resist endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), yet conventional transcriptomics measures gene abundance rather than isoform composition. Here, using endothelial-specific Esco2 deletion in a mouse model relevant to Roberts syndrome, we show that Esco2 loss causes yolk sac vascular remodeling failure, pathological EndMT, diversion from hemogenic endothelial fate, hemogenic endothelial depletion, impaired hematopoietic output, and embryonic lethality. Short-read single-cell RNA-seq revealed broad endothelial reprogramming, whereas single-cell long-read isoform sequencing uncovered a hidden layer of isoform dysregulation that conventional gene-level analysis failed to resolve. Esco2-deficient endothelium exhibited transcriptome-wide isoform switching, disruption of a multi-tier splicing-factor network, and predicted broad loss or rewiring of protein-coding output. Chromatin occupancy profiling localized Esco2 to exonic regions near alternatively spliced loci, supporting a cotranscriptional route to spliceopathy. Whole-genome sequencing showed that local DNA variation was insufficient to explain these changes, supporting a predominantly posttranscriptional mechanism. These findings identify isoform control as a disease-relevant layer of endothelial identity maintenance in Roberts syndrome.

title: Genomic, single-cell, and functional profiling of the CD48-CD244 axis and NK cell dysfunction in multiple myeloma.
abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) orchestrates immune evasion by subverting natural killer (NK) cell function. CD48, one of the most abundant NK ligands on MM cells, paradoxically enhances NK cell activation yet is associated with high-risk cytogenetics and poor patient survival. We integrated multiomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing [ATAC-seq], chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing [ChIP-seq]), genome-wide CRISPR knockout/activation screens, and machine learning to dissect CD48 regulation and function. In human MM and Vκ*MYC mouse scRNA-seq datasets, NK cells exhibit stepwise increases in inflammatory and exhaustion signatures and loss of cytotoxic potential as disease progresses. In vitro coculture assays show that CD48 overexpression on MM enhances NK cell cytokine secretion, whereas chronic exposure leads to ex vivo NK dysfunction. In vivo, CD48-overexpressing Vκ*MYC tumors progress more slowly and extend host survival, while NK cell depletion accelerates disease. These findings support a context-dependent role for CD48, potentiating acute NK responses while coexisting with chronic NK exhaustion, and suggest strategies to modulate CD48 for therapeutic benefit.

title: Integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses reveal UTF1-associated spermatogenic dysfunction and identify ACTRT2 and AKAP4 as biomarkers in non-obstructive azoospermia.
abstract: Non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) is a severe male infertility disorder caused by spermatogenic failure, and UTF1 is critical for maintaining undifferentiated spermatogonia and regulating germ cell development. This study aimed to explore the role of UTF1-related spermatogenic dysfunction in NOA and identify potential diagnostic biomarkers. We integrated NOA transcriptomic datasets with single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from Utf1 conditional knockout and normal mouse testes. Bioinformatic analyses and machine learning were applied to screen biomarkers, while functional enrichment, immune infiltration, cell-cell communication, and pseudotime trajectory analyses were performed together with histological validation in Utf1-deficient testes. Spermatogonia, Sertoli cells, and spermatids were identified as key cell populations. ACTRT2 and AKAP4 were confirmed as consistently downregulated NOA biomarkers and were integrated into a well-calibrated nomogram. These two genes were associated with cytoskeletal remodeling and meiotic regulation. NOA was also characterized by altered immune infiltration and cell-cell communication, whereas Utf1 deficiency impaired testicular development and spermatogenesis. Collectively, UTF1 deficiency was closely associated with spermatogenic dysfunction and microenvironmental remodeling in NOA, while ACTRT2 and AKAP4 might serve as potential diagnostic biomarkers of this process. These findings provide new insights into the molecular basis of NOA and may support future disease stratification and targeted intervention strategies.

title: RNA sequencing and proteomic analysis of diagnostic biopsies from colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are two of the most frequently occurring and lethal cancers. Although numerous studies have investigated their transcriptional, molecular, and immunological landscapes, our current understanding remains incomplete. Both cancers pose major clinical challenges, and better understanding of their molecular and immunological profiles is needed to improve patient outcomes. We conducted total RNA sequencing and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry-based proteomic profiling of 29 diagnostic biopsies from both primary tumors and metastatic sites in 16 CRC and 11 PDAC patients. Due to a lack of tissue, PDAC primary tumors were only analyzed by proteomics. Data analysis involved RNA-to-protein correlation analysis, multidimensional scaling, sample-to-sample Pearson correlations visualized as heatmaps with unsupervised clustering, differential expression analysis, gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis, and immune cell deconvolution using CIBERSORTx. Analyzing all available biopsies, RNA sequencing identified 46,492 expressed transcripts and proteomic analysis detected 6973 proteins, with 5563 genes common to both datasets. The mean absolute RNA-to-protein Spearman correlation was 0.241. In CRC, exploratory differential expression analysis identified 5 transcripts and 99 proteins differing between metastases and primary tumors. In PDAC, metastasis-to-primary tumor comparison was limited to proteomics and identified 305 differentially expressed proteins. In unsupervised clustering based on sample-to-sample correlation, CRC and PDAC biopsies formed two separate clusters. GO enrichment analysis demonstrated distinct patterns of up- and downregulation across molecular functions, cellular components, and biological processes in metastases compared with primary tumors. Inferred immune cell fractions indicated high levels of CD4 T memory resting cells and M0 macrophages. This exploratory study supports the feasibility of combined RNA sequencing and proteomic profiling from limited FFPE diagnostic biopsies and highlights proteomics as an important complement to transcriptomics. These findings enhance our understanding of biological and immunological heterogeneity and require further validation in larger independent cohorts for future development of prognostic markers and novel immunotherapeutic strategies.

title: Can arid1a expression levels in gastric carcinomas predict response to neoadjuvant therapy and prognosis?
abstract: The study aims to evaluate the significance of ARID1A expression in gastric cancer (GC) patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy, using immunohistochemical methods and bioinformatics approaches. Immunohistochemical analysis of an institutional clinical cohort (n = 80) was combined with bioinformatics analyses of independent public datasets. RNA-sequencing and clinical data from the TCGA-STAD cohort were retrieved and processed using TCGAbiolinks, differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2, and overall survival (OS) was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, and univariate Cox regression analyses. STRING was used to construct an ARID1A-centered protein association network, while Human Protein Atlas and Cellosaurus data were used to evaluate ARID1A expression. Loss of ARID1A protein expression rate was 41.3%. ARID1A loss and larger tumor size were correlated (median 6.0 cm vs. 4.0 cm; p = 0.004). ARID1A status and histopathological response to neoadjuvant therapy, pathological tumor stage and OS are not statistically related. Bioinformatics analyses demonstrated marked variation in ARID1A expression across GC cell lines, while TCGA-STAD analyses showed no significant tumor-normal difference or survival association at the transcript level. While ARID1A loss is associated with increased tumor size, it is not a strong independent predictor of treatment response or OS in GC. These findings underscore the molecular complexity of gastric adenocarcinoma and the need for larger, multicenter studies to refine the clinical utility of ARID1A.
